material_decisions.answer: Each endpoint delivery has at most 6 automatic attempts including the initial attempt. Connection refusal, DNS failure, connect timeout, TLS failure, response timeout, HTTP 408, HTTP 425, HTTP 429, and HTTP 5xx consume an attempt and are retryable. Other HTTP 4xx responses consume an attempt and immediately make the delivery terminally failed. A complete 2xx response makes it succeeded. Redirects are not followed and are treated as terminal 4xx-class failures. Retryable outcomes schedule delays of 10, 30, 120, 600, and 3600 seconds after attempts 1 through 5, measured from completion of the preceding attempt. For 429 or 503, a valid Retry-After value replaces the scheduled delay only when it is between 1 and 3600 seconds; otherwise the normal delay applies. No seventh automatic attempt is created.
material_decisions.why_material: This fixes delivery volume, latency, terminal-state timing, and behavior for every required failure class.

material_decisions.answer: Send the exact persisted UTF-8 JSON byte sequence as the HTTP body without reserialization or content encoding. Required headers are Webhook-Id containing the immutable event UUID, Webhook-Timestamp containing base-10 Unix seconds, and Webhook-Signature containing comma-separated v1=<lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256> entries. The signed byte sequence is the ASCII string Webhook-Id, a period, Webhook-Timestamp, a period, and the exact body bytes. Header names are case-insensitive, but values are not trimmed or normalized before verification. Verification requires all three headers, rejects timestamps more than 300 seconds from receiver time, and succeeds if any v1 signature matches any currently accepted secret using constant-time comparison. During rotation, both old and new secrets are accepted for 24 hours; the sender signs new attempts only with the new secret after rotation begins. Each retry gets a fresh timestamp and signature over the unchanged persisted body and event ID.
material_decisions.why_material: This makes signatures reproducible across byte encodings, retries, timestamp checks, and secret rotation.

material_decisions.answer: Webhook-Id is an immutable UUID assigned once to the logical account event and is the receiver-facing idempotency key. Automatic retries and manual replays preserve it. A distinct event always receives a distinct UUID even if its payload is byte-identical. Receivers deduplicate by the tuple of sender tenant identifier and Webhook-Id for 30 days after first successful processing. The same event sent to multiple endpoints retains its Webhook-Id, while sender-side delivery state is keyed separately by event ID and endpoint ID. Changing or replacing an endpoint creates a new endpoint delivery but does not create a new event identity. A manual replay after 30 days may be processed again and must be labeled as outside the promised deduplication window.
material_decisions.why_material: This prevents retries from causing duplicate side effects without suppressing distinct events or conflating endpoint delivery records.

material_decisions.answer: Store one logical delivery record per event-and-endpoint pair and one immutable attempt record per actual HTTP attempt. Delivery states are pending, retry_scheduled, in_flight, succeeded, and failed_exhausted; a terminal non-retryable client response uses failed_permanent. Each attempt records its sequential number, trigger type (automatic or manual), scheduled time, start and finish times, outcome class, HTTP status when available, sanitized error, signature key version, and next-retry time. Manual replay creates a new replay run linked to the original delivery, preserves the event ID, starts attempt numbering at 1 within that run, and never rewrites prior records. The operator view shows the current logical state, every run and attempt in order, the reason for each transition, and correlation IDs that map visible entries to worker and request logs.
material_decisions.why_material: This gives operators an auditable mapping from lifecycle state to every real attempt, retry, terminal outcome, and replay.

material_decisions.answer: The mandatory end-to-end test uses a receiver that verifies the signature, records the event ID and side effect, then drops the first response after processing. The sender must record attempt 1 as a response timeout, schedule and execute attempt 2 with the same event ID and body but a fresh valid timestamp and signature, and finish succeeded after the receiver returns 200. The receiver must record exactly one business side effect and one duplicate suppression. History must show both attempt records, their outcome classes and timestamps, the retry transition, and the final succeeded state. A subsequent manual replay must remain linked to the original delivery, use the same event ID, be visibly labeled manual, and cause no second business side effect within the 30-day window.
material_decisions.why_material: This proves the combined retry, authentication, idempotency, terminal-state, and operator-history guarantees under a realistic partial failure.

question.prompt: When an account event is accepted, what endpoint state should be frozen for its automatic deliveries? This determines whether later endpoint edits or rotations can redirect or alter already-queued requests.

options.label: Freeze full delivery config
options.description: Snapshot eligible endpoint IDs, destination URLs, and signing-key versions per delivery; later changes affect only new events, giving queued deliveries deterministic behavior.

options.label: Freeze membership only
options.description: Snapshot which endpoints receive the event but resolve their current URL and signing configuration at attempt time, allowing edits to affect queued deliveries.

options.label: Resolve everything later
options.description: Workers use endpoint membership and configuration current at execution time, reducing snapshots but allowing edits or disablement to change event fanout.

transcript.answer: Freeze full delivery config. When the account event is accepted, snapshot each eligible endpoint’s immutable endpoint ID, destination URL, and signing-key version into its event-and-endpoint delivery record. Automatic attempts and their scheduling use that snapshot, so later endpoint edits, deletion, or signing-key rotation affect only deliveries created for new events and cannot redirect or alter an already-queued delivery. Endpoint disablement is the exception: it cancels that endpoint’s scheduled future attempts without deleting or rewriting existing delivery or attempt history. Manual replay remains linked to the original delivery and event ID but creates a new run using the endpoint configuration and active signing key selected at replay initiation; that replay configuration is then frozen for the run and displayed in history.

question.prompt: Which receiver-facing signature envelope should be authoritative? This determines interoperable verification, replay protection, tenant scoping, and how receivers select the snapshotted signing secret.

options.label: Explicit versioned headers

question.prompt: During signing-secret rotation, which overlap model is authoritative? This determines whether queued deliveries signed under a frozen old key remain verifiable and how comma-separated v1 signatures are generated.

options.label: Dual-sign overlap
options.description: For a bounded rotation window, sign each attempt with both its snapshotted key and the endpoint’s active key, then retire the old key only after the window and all old-key deliveries are terminal; this eases receiver migration but requires protected access to both secrets.

options.label: Snapshot key only
options.description: Sign each automatic delivery only with its frozen key, requiring receivers to retain every old secret until all associated deliveries are terminal; simplest sender behavior but makes receiver rotation coordination stricter.

options.label: Active key only
options.description: Always sign attempts with the currently active key despite the delivery snapshot, simplifying receiver retention but contradicting the confirmed immutable signing configuration and changing queued deliveries after rotation.

transcript.answer: Use a 24-hour verification overlap, but do not dual-sign. Once rotation begins, every newly started attempt—including attempts for queued deliveries whose delivery record snapshots the old key version—is signed only with the new active secret. Receivers accept signatures from both the old and new secrets for 24 hours, after which the old secret is retired. Webhook-Signature therefore contains one v1 entry per attempt under normal rotation; comma-separated entries remain a verification format, not a requirement to emit both rotation keys. The delivery snapshot remains immutable historical configuration, while the rotation rule explicitly governs attempt-time signing.

question.prompt: Which outbound destination policy must webhook endpoints follow? This determines whether tenant-controlled URLs can reach internal infrastructure and what validation workers must repeat before every connection.

options.label: Public HTTPS only
options.description: Require HTTPS, block loopback/link-local/private/reserved IP ranges after DNS resolution, re-resolve and revalidate every attempt, connect only to the validated address, and continue to prohibit redirects; strongest production isolation with no private-network destinations.

options.label: Public HTTP or HTTPS
options.description: Apply the same IP and DNS-rebinding protections but permit plaintext HTTP, improving local compatibility while exposing webhook bodies and signatures to network interception.

options.label: Private destinations allowed
options.description: Permit private or internal addresses through explicit tenant allowlists, enabling intranet integrations but requiring materially broader network isolation, authorization, auditing, and support controls.

transcript.answer: Public HTTPS only. Webhook endpoint URLs must use HTTPS. On every delivery attempt, resolve the destination hostname, reject loopback, link-local, private, reserved, multicast, and otherwise non-public IP addresses, and connect only to the validated resolved address. Repeat DNS resolution and IP validation before every connection to prevent DNS rebinding. Do not follow redirects; treat them as terminal failures under the established outcome policy. Private or internal destinations and plaintext HTTP are not permitted.

Delivery-history audience, tenant/support permissions, filters, statuses, exposed request/response details, and support actions
Manual replay authorization, endpoint/config selection permissions, rate limits, and audit fields
Numeric connection and response timeouts
Payload envelope schema, event-type/versioning rules, and maximum payload size
Persistence entities, uniqueness constraints, lifecycle states, retention, payload redaction, audit requirements, and deletion behavior
Receiver behavior for manual replay when Webhook-Id is reused: suppress previously processed events or deliberately process them again
Secret storage protection, disclosure rules, emergency revocation behavior, and operator permissions
Sender API boundaries for endpoint configuration and verification, outbox integration, validation, quotas, and authorization
Tenant isolation, quotas, rate limiting, and abuse protections beyond the confirmed public-HTTPS SSRF policy
Worker concurrency limits, leasing, crash recovery, scheduling, terminal/dead-letter behavior, scaling, observability, and SLO expectations

question.prompt: When a manual replay reuses an already processed Webhook-Id, what must receivers do? This determines whether replay can repeat business effects or is only a safe redelivery that receivers may suppress.

options.label: Deduplicate replay
options.description: Receivers apply the same tenant-plus-Webhook-Id deduplication to automatic attempts and manual replays; replay verifies transport and can recover only when the original event was not recorded as processed.

options.label: Process replay again
options.description: Receivers must distinguish a replay and intentionally process it again despite the reused Webhook-Id, requiring a new authenticated replay indicator and receiver-side safeguards.

options.label: Issue new ID
options.description: Manual replay receives a new Webhook-Id linked to the original, enabling ordinary processing but revising the confirmed rule that replays preserve the original identity.

transcript.answer: Receivers must apply the same sender-tenant-plus-Webhook-Id deduplication to manual replays as to automatic retries. Within the 30-day deduplication window, an already processed event must be suppressed and must not repeat business effects. After that window, a replay may be processed again and must be labeled as outside the promised deduplication window.

question.prompt: Which JSON envelope must every webhook use? This fixes the receiver contract and the immutable body bytes persisted and signed for all attempts and replays.

options.label: Versioned envelope
options.description: Use a stable envelope containing id, type, version, occurred_at, account_id, and data; evolve event payloads through explicit per-type integer versions while keeping the envelope backward compatible.

options.label: CloudEvents JSON
options.description: Adopt the structured CloudEvents JSON format and place the product payload in data; improves standards interoperability but adds a broader external specification and compatibility surface.

options.label: Event-specific body
options.description: Send each event's fields at the JSON root with only minimal shared metadata; produces smaller payloads but weakens uniform parsing and version evolution.

output.answer: Versioned envelope. Every webhook body is a stable UTF-8 JSON envelope containing id, type, version, occurred_at, account_id, and data. The id equals the immutable Webhook-Id UUID, type identifies the event type, version is an integer version scoped to that event type, occurred_at is the event occurrence timestamp, account_id identifies the sender tenant account, and data contains the event-specific payload. Envelope fields remain backward compatible, while incompatible event payload changes require a new per-type version. The exact serialized envelope bytes are persisted once and reused unchanged for every automatic attempt and manual replay.
